title: What the Practical Measures, and How It Is Graded
subtitle: The arithmetic that governs every strategic decision you make in the room.
summary: The practical does not reward a single brilliant flight. It rewards competence held steady across twelve wines and three days. A pass is a 65% average across the three papers with a roughly 50% floor under any one of them, criterion-referenced — an absolute bar, not a curve. This chapter installs that arithmetic, separates what is confirmed from what is only plausible, and dismantles the most damaging misreading of the rule: that you need 65% on every paper.

blocks.md: The examiner is not marking your library. They are watching three things, in order, on every wine you touch.

The practical measures whether you can do three named things: **assess the wine** in the glass accurately; **reach a sound judgement** from that assessment — quality, origin, variety, maturity, winemaking, commercial position; and **communicate it concisely** under brutal time pressure. Three abilities. Not four. Identification is part of the second — it is necessary, but it is never sufficient.

blocks.title: Three abilities, not four
blocks.md: You will sometimes see the practical described as a test of "four dimensions." That is a tidy reconstruction, not what the IMW publishes. The Institute's own stated framework is three abilities: assess, judge, communicate. Theory accuracy is best treated as a discipline that runs underneath all three — not as a fourth thing the exam scores in its own column.

This matters because of *how* the three combine. A pass is a **minimum across the abilities, not an average of them**. A spike in one cannot rescue a hole in another. You do not pass by tasting brilliantly and writing incoherently, or by writing beautifully about a wine you have misread. Each ability has to clear a bar of its own.
The exam tests competence held across three abilities — assess, judge, communicate — and a spike in one never pays for a hole in another.

sections.title: The pass standard: a 65% average, not 65% per paper

blocks.md: Learn the arithmetic exactly, because nearly every strategic decision in the room descends from it.

A pass is a **65% average across the three practical papers** — Paper 1 whites, Paper 2 reds, Paper 3 the mixed special. It is **not** 65% on every paper. The three scores are averaged, and the average has to reach 65.

blocks.title: The rule, verbatim
blocks.md: The IMW Student Guide states it directly: *"To pass the practical component you need to average 65% or more across all three papers, with a minimum of 50% in any one paper."* That single sentence carries both halves of the pass standard — the average and the floor.

The standard is **criterion-referenced**: an absolute bar, not a curve. You are not competing against the cohort for a fixed number of passes. You are measured against a fixed standard of competence. A weak year does not lower the bar to let you through, and a strong year does not raise it to keep you out.

Because the average governs, **a strong paper can carry a weaker one above the line** — provided the weaker paper still clears its floor. This is the single most important strategic consequence of the arithmetic, and it is the exact opposite of what "65% per paper" would have you believe. You are not defending three independent thresholds. You are defending one aggregate, with a tripwire under each paper.

blocks.title: One answer is a fragment of a paper
blocks.md: No single wine decides your band. A paper is twelve wines; the band is an aggregate of three papers. So treat any one answer as exactly that — a fragment. A weak response on one wine is not a failed paper; it is a few marks you now have to make up across the eleven that remain. Judge yourself on the paper, then on the three-paper average — never on a single flight.
Pass = 65% average across the three papers, criterion-referenced — so a strong paper can carry a weaker one, never "65% on every paper."
The average is the goal. The floor is the tripwire. They are different gates, and the floor does not care how high your average is.

Every single paper must clear a minimum floor of **~50%**. The Student Guide says "minimum of 50% in any one paper." A handful of candidate accounts cite 55%, which is why the "~" is worth keeping — but the Guide's number is 50, and the existence of the floor is not in doubt.

blocks.title: The floor is an independent gate
blocks.md: A paper that falls below ~50% **cannot be rescued by a high average**. The carry-the-weaker-paper move works *only while every paper stays above the floor*. Bank all the strong papers you like; the moment one paper breaches ~50%, the average stops mattering and you fail the practical. Treat the floor as a hard line you protect on Paper 3 especially, where the unfamiliar styles live.

There is a second, softer line further down. The 2022 Practical Chair's predecessor in 2018 noted that candidates who land **below an average of 45% across their practical papers "almost never go on to pass" — "less than 5%."** Read this correctly: it is an **aggregate tendency across the papers, not a per-paper rule**, and the staged way the exam is sat softens it further. It is simply the altitude below which the climb back rarely happens.
Banking strong papers works only while every paper clears the ~50% floor; one paper below it is fatal regardless of the average.
Above the pass line sit the bands. Know which of them you can trust as fact, and which rest on a source nobody can quite read.

The bands run, from the top: **A** at 70 and above; **B** at 65–69; **C+** at 60–64, the borderline band; and below that, fail. The bands are defined on the **aggregate** across all three papers, not per paper.

blocks.title: C+ = 60–64 is confirmed
blocks.md: The C+ borderline band is the one band that is report-verified, from two independent sources: the IMW Student Guide and the 2024 MW Practical report, in which Peter Marks MW defines "the C+ or 60% – 64% range across all three papers." Treat 60–64 = C+ as solid.

blocks.title: A ≥ 70 and B 65–69 are plausible only — do not treat them as fact
blocks.md: The A and B cut-points come from a single place: an image-based examiner appendix that is **unreadable**. Only the appendix heading extracts; the band numbers themselves cannot be read off it, and no readable report confirms them. We hold them at roughly 65% confidence, against 95% for the averaging headline. So: use them as a working ladder, but **never present A ≥ 70 or B 65–69 as confirmed.** They are indicative, not verified.

blocks.md: Hold that hedge deliberately. The point of the band ladder is to orient you — not to hand you false precision about where distinction begins. You know exactly where the borderline sits; you do **not** know, to the point, where an A starts.
Only C+ = 60–64 is confirmed; the A ≥ 70 and B 65–69 edges are plausible, resting on an unreadable appendix — use them, never assert them.
"65% to pass" has a natural reading and a correct one, and they are not the same. The natural reading is the dangerous one.

When you hear "you need 65%," the obvious inference is **65% on every paper** — three separate hurdles, each at 65. That inference is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that costs marks. The rule is a 65% **average** across the three papers, with a **~50% floor** under any single one. The word doing the work is *average*, and the natural reading quietly deletes it.

blocks.title: Why the misreading is costly, not just inaccurate
blocks.md: "65% per paper" teaches the wrong strategy. It implies every paper — and by proxy every answer — must independently hit 65, which **discourages the correct play**: bank your strong papers to carry a weaker one above the average, while never letting any paper breach the ~50% floor. A candidate who believes the hurdle version over-defends a paper that is already safe and panics over an average that is already passing. The arithmetic you carry into the room changes how you spend twelve minutes per wine.

So fix the reading once: **one aggregate at 65, three tripwires at ~50.** That is the whole governing rule, and it is the opposite of three hurdles at 65. Internalise it now, because under exam pressure you will default to whatever model you walked in with.

blocks.title: The borderline candidate and the theory howler
blocks.md: One examiner behaviour is worth carrying into this. When a script's aggregate lands at the **borderline** and a clear **theory howler** is present — an obvious, indefensible error of fact — the examiners resolve the borderline downward, to a fail, and name it. They withhold the benefit of the doubt from a borderline candidate making an obvious theory mistake. This is exam reality, drawn from the examiner reports: at the margin, an unforced howler is not a rounding error — it is the thing that tips you the wrong way.
The rule is one average at 65 plus three floors at ~50 — not 65 on every paper; and at the borderline, a clear theory howler resolves the script to a fail.

sections.title: Distinction is consistency, not one brilliant flight

blocks.md: The top of the ladder is not won by a single dazzling wine. It is won by never having a weak one.

High marks — and distinction in particular — appear to reward **consistency across all three papers** rather than one brilliant script. This is directionally supported, not a hard, scored rule: nobody hands out marks for "consistency" in a column of its own. It is the shape that high-scoring scripts tend to take — even across, with no weak section — not a lever you can pull on a single wine.

blocks.title: The 2022 Practical Chair, verbatim
blocks.md: *"There were no high pass marks, which demonstrates that one off-day will not ruin one's chances, but consistency is essential."* — 2022 Practical Chair report. Read as a year in which, with passes awarded, no candidate scored an A at all. The report itself says "no high pass marks"; the "no A" reading is a plausible interpretation of that, not a flat published statistic.

Read the Chair's two clauses together, because they cut both ways. "One off-day will not ruin one's chances" is the floor-and-average arithmetic being kind to you — a single weak flight need not sink the average. "Consistency is essential" is the price of the top band: the A comes from **no weak section across twelve wines and three days**, not from one virtuoso flight carrying a weak paper. The same year that forgives an off-day refuses to hand out a high pass to anyone who was merely brilliant once.
Distinction rewards consistency across twelve wines and three days, not one peak flight — a directional truth about high-scoring scripts, not a mark awarded on a single wine.
